The patient is a 17-year-old male with **acute, localized mucosal bleeding after minor oral surgery**, refractory to standard pressure. Lab findings show an **isolated, significantly prolonged aPTT (60 sec)** with normal PT, normal platelet count, mildly low hematocrit (likely due to recent blood loss), and borderline-prolonged bleeding time. This pattern — isolated aPTT elevation + mucosal (not deep tissue/joint) bleeding — strongly favors a **mild intrinsic pathway defect affecting early hemostasis at the level of platelet–vessel wall interaction or Factor VIII/vWF function**, rather than severe hemophilia A (which typically presents earlier with hemarthroses or post-traumatic hematomas) or Factor IX deficiency (hemophilia B, which also usually manifests before adolescence with more severe bleeding). Von Willebrand disease (vWD) — particularly **Type 1 (partial quantitative deficiency)** — is the **most common inherited bleeding disorder**, highly prevalent (~1% population), often undiagnosed until provoked by dental procedures, and classically presents with mucocutaneous bleeding (e.g., epistaxis, menorrhagia, post-extraction bleeding) and isolated aPTT prolongation (due to reduced FVIII stabilization by vWF) plus abnormal bleeding time/PFA-100.
